1 · Hackathon brief

Transport Stack Hackathon 2026 — Full Brief

Captured 2026-11-11 from: - https://whereuelevate.com/drills/transport-stack-hackathon-2026 (registration / listing) - https://delhi.transportstack.in/hackathon/ (official problem briefs)

Overview

Build open-source tools using real Delhi transit data. Teams tackle five problems built on live bus GPS, e-ticketing, Electronic Ticketing Machine (ETM) records, and metro Automatic Fare Collection (AFC) records.

  • Organizer: Transport Stack — an initiative by the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), run by Chartr with the Centre for Sustainable Mobility (CSM), IIIT Delhi, and owned by the Airawat Research Foundation (ARF), IIT Kanpur.
  • Cost: Free
  • Format: Problem-based innovation, two online phases + hybrid finale
  • Team size: 2–3 members
  • Total prizes: ₹275,000
  • Best solutions may be taken forward as open-source components on Transport Stack.

Eligibility

Open to everyone — students, researchers, startups, and working professionals, in India or abroad — in teams of 2–3 members. One member registers the team and adds the others. The form enforces the 2–3 member limit.

Key Dates & Timeline

⚠️ Date discrepancy between sources — confirm with organizers. The WhereUElevate listing's description mentions the Annual Event on 10 Dec 2026, but its own timeline and the official site both state the finale is 11 Dec 2026.

Stage Dates Mode Notes
Registration Until 20 Nov 2026, 23:59 IST Online Register team on Where U Elevate
Phase 1 — Prototype Submission 29 Oct 2026, 1:30 PM IST → 25 Nov 2026 (~2 weeks) Online Open to all registered teams. Pick Problem 1 or 2; submit proposal + working prototype + code repo URL
Phase 2 — Build Sprint 25 Nov 2026 → 10 Dec 2026 (~2 weeks) Online Shortlisted teams only. Refine Phase 1 work OR take on Problem 3, 4 or 5. Weekly 10–15 min mentor session
Phase 3 — Finale & Winners 11 Dec 2026, 1:30–5:30 PM IST Hybrid Present Phase 2 solutions; judged at Transport Stack Annual Event, IIIT Delhi, Okhla Phase III, New Delhi
  • ~10–12 teams shortlisted for Phase 2 (expected field of 200+ teams).
  • No on-site building round — both build phases are online.

Submission Requirements

Phase 1 (all teams): Pick Problem 1 or Problem 2 and submit: - A proposal - A working prototype (mock-only or slide-only submissions do NOT qualify) - Working code repository URL

Every submission requires: - Source code with a README - A short technical note - A short demo video

Solutions must be original team work. Open-source libraries and AI tools are allowed as long as they are credited.

Judging Criteria (indicative)

  • Problem relevance
  • Technical depth and correct use of the data
  • Feasibility
  • Innovation
  • Usability and impact

Each problem brief also lists its own success criteria.

Ownership

Teams keep credit for their work. Standout solutions may be taken forward as open-source components on Transport Stack and used for Delhi's buses and metro.

The Five Problems

Phase 1 (open to all teams)

Problem 1 — Real-time bus traffic model and journey planner

  • Background. Delhi's buses generate continuous location data across the city's road network. Combined with historical patterns, this can model traffic flow and travel times, making the bus fleet a strong proxy for services like Google Maps.
  • Challenge. Build a traffic model from real-time and historical bus location data and integrate it with a journey-planning interface. Goal: a Google Maps-like API that estimates bus travel times between any two locations.
  • Data. Historical and real-time bus location data for Delhi: GPS traces, route information, stop locations.
  • Success criteria. A working API that takes two locations and returns plausible bus journey options with estimated travel times. Estimates should hold up against known actual travel times for sample location pairs and against Google Maps.
  • Full brief: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1rfEu-ptgN4MNlcTKvv59nzc_OVjPmbk_hAxpe5HCirc/preview

Problem 2 — Crowdedness-aware journey planner

  • Background. Crowdedness shapes how commuters experience a trip, yet existing journey planners ignore it. E-ticketing and ETM data make it possible to estimate how crowded buses are across routes and times of day.
  • Challenge. Build a model that estimates crowdedness across bus routes and times of day from ~4–5 weeks of e-ticketing and ETM data, then integrate it into a journey planner so commuters can choose routes on both travel time and expected crowdedness.
  • Data. E-ticketing and ETM data for 4–5 weeks (ticket sales, routes, timestamps). Route and stop information from Transport Stack.
  • Success criteria. A journey planner that shows crowdedness estimates alongside route options. Estimates should be grounded in the ticketing data and hold up when spot-checked against known peak and off-peak patterns.
  • Full brief: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ocS9rG4_E_Fb9DJcqTG8SClrLJJ_UJqGGAhgPbV8tr4/preview

Phase 2 (shortlisted teams)

Problem 3 — Origin–destination (OD) matrix for Delhi public transit

  • Background. Knowing where trips start and end is the foundation of transit planning. Delhi has two partial views: bus e-ticketing data (captures only 3–4% of bus tickets) and metro gate data (far more complete).
  • Challenge. Estimate an OD matrix for Delhi's public transit network that matches real-world travel as closely as possible. Core problem is extrapolation: scaling a small bus e-ticketing sample to full ridership, using the denser metro data to inform travel density across the city.
  • Data. Bus e-ticketing data, metro entry/exit gate data, and route/stop information from Transport Stack.
  • Success criteria. A reproducible OD matrix at stop or zone level, with a documented extrapolation method. Results should be consistent with known ridership totals and metro gate counts; the method should state its assumptions and where uncertainty is highest.
  • Full brief: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QqegxZ79vmf1t50RAekK3Q2hjJzltBmxgeS7pNoiSvg/preview

Problem 4 — Feeder bus routes for metro stations

  • Background. Many metro riders struggle with the first/last mile between the station and home or work. A well-planned feeder network extends the reach of every station, but only if routes fit real road conditions and the operating limits of an electric fleet.
  • Challenge. Design feeder routes for a given list of metro stations using a fleet of ~500 electric buses, maximising coverage. Use metro entry/exit data to decide where demand is, and plan around charging needs. Constraints:
  • Maximum route length of 7 km (local service only)
  • Account for traffic conditions
  • Use only roads wider than 6 metres on each side
  • Data. List of target metro stations, metro entry/exit data, road network data, and bus traffic/stop information from Transport Stack.
  • Success criteria. A set of feeder routes with fleet allocation that respects every constraint, plus clear coverage metrics (e.g. share of population or metro demand served). The charging plan should be feasible for the proposed schedules.
  • Full brief: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QzjMaB5KwvXAQ8xU1tZuiJOcm4z9mqDsCIk-e7SjkYQ/preview

Problem 5 — Metro and bus crowding estimation

  • Background. AFC systems record where passengers board and alight. Across a full month, this data can show how passenger load builds and falls along each line and route — useful for operators (capacity planning) and commuters (trip planning).
  • Challenge. Estimate crowding levels on Delhi's metro and buses from historical AFC boarding/alighting data. Produce load estimates by line or route, segment, and time of day.
  • Data. ~1 month of AFC boarding and alighting data, plus route, stop and station information from Transport Stack.
  • Success criteria. Crowding estimates by segment and time band that can be queried or visualised. The method for turning boarding/alighting records into on-vehicle load should be documented; results should match known peak and off-peak patterns.
  • Full brief: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1fVuVjfvWTp5NVlcT52liQEipbwBfkQl-k0GnTAd3a0A/preview

Available Datasets

Sign up on the Delhi Transport Stack platform and request the datasets your problem needs. Available for the hackathon:

  • Real-time bus positions (GTFS-RT) for DTC and cluster buses, updated every few seconds
  • Historical bus GPS traces covering several weeks
  • Static bus GTFS: ~10,500 stops, ~2,400 routes, ~89,000 scheduled trips
  • E-ticketing and ETM data covering 4–5 weeks
  • Metro entry and exit (gate) data
  • ~1 month of AFC boarding and alighting data
  • Road network data and the list of target metro stations (Problem 4)

2 · Prototype plan

Prototype Plan — Problem 2: Crowdedness-Aware Journey Planner

Phase 1 deliverable for the Transport Stack Hackathon 2026. Target problem: Problem 2. See HACKATHON.md for the brief. Planning date: 2026-11-11 · Phase 1 deadline: 25 Nov 2026 (~2 weeks).

1. The product in one sentence

A journey planner that, for a trip from A to B, returns bus route options ranked on both estimated travel time and expected crowdedness — where crowdedness is estimated from Delhi's e-ticketing / ETM data by time of day.

2. Who it's for & why it matters

  • Commuter: "Which bus should I take — and will I get a seat / be able to board?" Today's planners answer when, never how packed.
  • Operator (secondary): sees where/when load concentrates → capacity planning.

The judged success criteria (from the brief) we must hit: 1. Planner shows crowdedness estimates alongside route options. 2. Estimates are grounded in the ticketing data. 3. Estimates hold up vs known peak / off-peak patterns (our validation story).

2b. Competitive landscape — existing Delhi journey planners

Researched 2026-11-11 (web). Takeaway: journey planning + live bus tracking for Delhi is a solved, crowded space; crowdedness grounded in the city's own ticketing data is an open white space. That is exactly where Problem 2 sits.

App Journey planning Live bus tracking Ticketing Crowdedness Notes
One Delhi (official GNCTD) ✅ universal planner ✅ 7,300+ DTC + cluster buses, real-time ETA ✅ QR, 10% e-ticket discount ❌ Built by Chartr with Transport Dept & IIIT-D — the same operator running this hackathon
Chalo ✅ ✅ GPS-based ETA ✅ passes + tickets ⚠️ "Live Passenger Indicator" in select cities only (Delhi unconfirmed) Real-time device-based occupancy
Tummoc ✅ patented multimodal (bus+metro+auto+cab) ✅ DTC live tracking ✅ all-in-one ticket ❌ Also shows cost + carbon saved
Google Maps ✅ ✅ live traffic delays for buses ❌ ⚠️ crowdedness predictions via opt-in crowdsourcing + AI/historical 100 countries; not grounded in Delhi ticketing
Moovit ✅ ✅ updated DTC feed — ⚠️ global crowdedness (APC sensors + ticket data + crowdsourcing); Delhi unconfirmed —
DMRC Momentum metro-focused — (metro) ✅ metro ❌ Official Delhi Metro app
Transport Stack Multimodal Journey Planner ✅ (API, approval-based) — — ❌ The hackathon's own platform API

How crowdedness is done elsewhere (and why ours differs)

  • Sensor-based (Moovit/Transit, Surat): automatic passenger counters (APC) on vehicles → direct but needs hardware Delhi's fleet largely lacks.
  • Crowdsourced (Google Maps): opt-in rider surveys + AI on historical trends → broad coverage but sparse, noisy, not tied to actual ridership.
  • Real-time device (Chalo): proprietary on-bus signals in select cities.
  • Ours (ticketing/ETM-grounded): estimate load from Delhi's actual e-ticketing + ETM boarding records — real ridership, open and reproducible, no extra hardware. This matches the brief's "grounded in the ticketing data" criterion and is not offered by any incumbent for Delhi.

Implications for our prototype

  1. Don't compete on travel-time/ETA — One Delhi, Google, Chalo, Tummoc, Moovit already do it well. (Reinforces choosing Problem 2 over Problem 1.)
  2. Crowdedness is the differentiator — and specifically ticketing-grounded crowdedness, which no Delhi planner surfaces.
  3. Complement, don't duplicate, One Delhi (same operator, Chartr) — frame our output as an open-source crowding component that could feed One Delhi / Transport Stack, aligning with the hackathon's "open-source component" goal.
  4. Benchmark opportunity: we can sanity-check our estimates against the qualitative crowd signals these apps expose and against known peak/off-peak patterns.

Sources (links verified 2026-11-11): One Delhi — Google Play, One Delhi — App Store, Chalo, Tummoc — Google Play, Moovit, Transit — crowding (sensor/ticket/crowdsource method), Google Maps crowdedness — Google Transit Partners, Surat real-time occupancy — Data for Public Good.

3. The core idea — how we turn tickets into crowding

Tickets record boardings (route, direction, boarding stop, timestamp, pax). On-vehicle load is a cumulative quantity along the route:

load(segment i→i+1) = Σ boardings at stops ≤ i  −  Σ alightings at stops ≤ i
crowding_index      = load / vehicle_capacity          # per bus type
crowding_level      = bucket(crowding_index)           # Low / Medium / High
  • Boardings come straight from ticket aggregation per (route, direction, stop, time-band).
  • Alightings — two cases:
  • If the ticket carries a fare stage / destination → alighting stop is known directly (best case).
  • If only boarding is recorded → estimate alightings with a simple model (e.g. distance-decay / proportional to downstream boarding demand), stated as an assumption.
  • Capacity by bus type (standard ~ seated+standing); documented constant to start.
  • Time-bands: 30- or 60-min buckets, by day-type (weekday / weekend).

This "boarding/alighting → load profile" method is the technical heart and the thing we document in the technical note.

Coverage note: e-ticketing alone captures only ~3–4% of bus tickets; ETM data is the higher-coverage source and should anchor the estimate. Scale/weight to known ridership where possible, and state uncertainty.

4. Scope

Note (2026-11-12): the earlier crowding model, ticket schema, and synthetic e-ticketing generator were removed — they were built on hypothetical data. We'll rebuild the ingestion + crowding model on the actual e-ticketing/ETM datasets once access lands. The method (Section 3) still stands as the design.

MVP (must-have for Phase 1)

  • [x] Ingest GTFS static (routes, stops, schedules) — src/data/gtfs.py (GTFSFeed).
  • [ ] Ingest real e-ticketing / ETM data (awaiting access) + define its schema.
  • [ ] Crowding model on real data → (route, segment, hour) → crowding level (boardings → alighting shape → per-vehicle load profile → level).
  • [ ] Journey endpoint: for an O→D, return candidate bus options with travel time (from GTFS schedule) + crowding level per option.
  • [ ] A ranking that trades off time vs crowding.
  • [ ] Validation: crowding peaks at rush hour, dips off-peak (on real data).
  • [ ] Map UI (Stage 2) showing options with a crowding badge + colour.

Stretch (if time allows)

  • Multi-leg / transfer journeys.
  • "Leave later for a less crowded bus" suggestion.
  • Confidence / uncertainty shown per estimate.
  • Real-time flavour by blending GTFS-RT positions (optional, P1 territory).
  • Multimodal (bus + metro) crowding view — organizer-encouraged (2026-11-12); layer metro crowding from footfall (datadetails/4) + OD (datadetails/9) on top of the bus baseline. Strong differentiator / likely bonus; pursue after the bus MVP.

Explicitly out of scope for Phase 1

  • Full multimodal routing / transfers as a core deliverable (bus-only crowding is the committed MVP; a metro crowding layer is the stretch above).
  • Production auth, scaling, polished design system.

Stack (per team strengths): Stage 1 = Python/data-science (pandas, scikit-learn, FastAPI, a Jupyter EDA/validation notebook). Stage 2 = React/Next.js with a map library. Keep the frontend talking to the API only — the model stays in Python.

6. Repo layout (target)

src/
  data/        # gtfs.py (done); tickets.py (ingest REAL e-ticketing/ETM — add with data)
  model/       # crowding.py (boarding→load→level) — build on real data

  web/         # Stage 2 frontend
notebooks/     # EDA findings & figures
data/          # raw datasets (gitignored) + data/README on how to fetch

7. Data plan & the gap

  • Available now (build immediately): GTFS static (bus routes/stops/schedules) — Open on the catalogue. Lets us build routing + the whole skeleton today.
  • Pending: e-ticketing / ETM — not in the public catalogue. Request email sent 2026-11-11; organizer replied 2026-11-12 that access is granted on request ("by today") — awaiting actual access. Still a critical-path risk until it lands.
  • Scope & datasets confirmed by organizer (2026-11-12):
  • Minimum scope is buses; a multimodal (bus + metro) view is encouraged (bonus, not required).
  • No other immediately relevant datasets beyond: bus GTFS, e-ticketing/ETM, metro hourly footfall (datadetails/4), metro yearly OD (datadetails/9). Others may be explored later in the hackathon.
  • → Committed MVP: bus-only crowding. Stretch: add a metro crowding layer for a multimodal view (would need the two metro datasets, both approval-based).
  • Approach while waiting (decided 2026-11-12): no synthetic stand-in — the crowding model will be built on the actual e-ticketing/ETM data to keep results credible. Meanwhile, make progress on the parts that need only GTFS: the journey-planner routing + schedule travel time. Crowding layers on once data lands.
